name: Cube-4 Memory Access Patterns
text:
# Cube-4 Memory Access Patterns

Also called: Cube-4 Skewed Memory

## Overview
Cube-4 Memory Access Patterns describe the memory stride characteristics of the Cube-4 skewed memory organization used in volume rendering hardware. The method solves the problem of mapping 3D voxel data to parallel memory modules to maximize bandwidth, but it introduces view-dependent access strides that can exceed DRAM page sizes. It is distinguished from sibling methods like [Skewed Memory Organization for Conflict-Free Ray Access](2351-skewed-memory-organization-for-conflict-free-ray-access.md) by its specific stride formulas ($1, N/C, N^2/C$) and its documented failure to utilize fast page mode for certain view directions due to these large strides [S1, unofficial].

## How it works
**Inputs:**
- $N$: The side length of the cubic dataset ($N^3$ voxels).
- $C$: The number of memory modules.
- View direction: Defined by the normal vector relative to the dataset axes (X, Y, or Z).

**Outputs:**
- Memory access stride for successive voxels in the rendering path.

**Data Structures:**
The memory is organized into $C$ modules. Voxels are assigned to modules based on the [Cube-4](#14515-cube-4.md) skewed addressing scheme. The specific addressing formula is not detailed in the provided sources, but the resulting access patterns are defined by the view direction.

**Steps and Formulas:**
1. Determine the view normal direction relative to the dataset axes.
2. Calculate the memory access stride $S$ based on the view direction:
   - If the view normal is parallel to the **Z axis**: $S = 1$.
   - If the view normal is parallel to the **X axis**: $S = N/C$.
   - If the view normal is parallel to the **Y axis**: $S = N^2/C$.
   [S1, unofficial]

3. **Access Pattern Details:**
   - **X-axis view (YZ face):** Successive voxels in successive partial beams parallel to the Y axis require a stride of $N/C$. There is an anomaly in this stride at the beginning of each beam.
   - **Y-axis view (ZX face):** Successive voxels of successive partial beams require a stride of $N^2/C$. There is an anomaly at the beginning of each beam.
   - **Z-axis view:** Stride is 1, allowing contiguous access.
   [S1, unofficial]

**Edge Cases and Pitfalls:**
- **DRAM Page Mode Failure:** For X-axis and Y-axis views, the strides $N/C$ and $N^2/C$ often exceed common DRAM page sizes. This precludes the use of fast page (column) mode access, reducing performance to random (row) access levels.
- **Anomaly at Beam Start:** The stride anomaly at the beginning of each partial beam limits the benefit of fast page mode, even for smaller strides.
- **View Dependence:** The system must handle the worst-case stride (typically Y-axis view) to maintain consistent performance targets, as performance varies significantly with view direction.
  [S1, unofficial]

## Subtopics

### Cube-4 Light
An improvement to the Cube-4 algorithm that allows perspective projections. It introduces view-dependent filtering artifacts.
[S2, unofficial]

## Operating characteristics
**Time and Memory Complexity:**
- The memory system must deliver a sustained bandwidth of 1 Gbyte/sec independent of view direction to meet performance targets.
- The memory capacity required is 32 Mbytes for the described implementation.
  [S1, unofficial]

**Measured Performance:**
- The view-dependent strides exceeding DRAM page sizes reduce achievable memory performance to random access levels for non-Z-axis views.
- The system design is forced to handle the worst-case view direction (Y-axis) to ensure consistent performance.
  [S1, unofficial]

**Strengths and Limitations:**
- **Strengths:** Provides a structured mapping for parallel memory access.
- **Limitations:** View-dependent performance degradation due to DRAM page mode incompatibility for X and Y axis views. The stride anomalies at beam beginnings further reduce efficiency.
  [S1, unofficial]

**When to Use/Not Use:**
- Use when Z-axis aligned views are dominant or when the hardware can tolerate random access penalties for other views.
- Not suitable when consistent high performance across all view directions is required without [hardware-specific optimizations](#10277-hardware-specific-optimization.md) to mitigate page mode failures.
  [S1, unofficial]

## Background
The Cube-4 memory access patterns were described in the context of the [EM-Cube architecture](#22564-em-cube-architecture.md), an architecture for low-cost real-time volume rendering. The work was published in 1997. The architecture was designed to meet specific performance targets for VLSI implementation, requiring high sustained bandwidth.
[S1, unofficial]

## Sources
[S1] EM-Cube: An Architecture for Low-Cost Real-Time Volume Rendering The Harvard community has made this article openly available..., https://vcg.seas.harvard.edu/publications/19970101-em-cube-an-architecture-for-low-cost-real-time-volume-rendering/paper, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
[S2] Real-Time Volume Rendering, https://cfcs.pku.edu.cn/baoquan/docs/20180622110335231616.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)
